title: Better governance scores predict worse shareholder returns—company decline is not inevitable
dek: Eric Ries uses data to counter the fatalism that "companies inevitably go bad as they grow": counterexamples like Costco and Patagonia violate nearly all traditional "best practices," proving corruption is not scale's inevitable cost but a preventable choice of governance structure.
why: 22-minute conversation with high information density, focused on governance score data and the historical origins of shareholder primacy, helping founders and investors quickly grasp a contrarian framework.
who: Founders fundraising, preparing for IPO, or planning acquisition; investors and board members designing company governance.
skip: The opening approximately two minutes of program introduction and mid-episode advertisements.

points.h: Financial gravity silently tilts decisions toward resource holders
points.body: Ries introduced "financial gravity"—a psychological pressure where values of those with resources flow one-way to those seeking them. Like the automatic deference shown to a billionaire, organizations develop unconscious patterns: people invoke "the market won't like this" or "donors might not like that" without actually asking either, just intuitive unexamined hunches acting like an invisible participant in every meeting.

points.h: Shareholder primacy is a recent legal invention, not tradition
points.body: Ries challenges the claim that "shareholder primacy is American tradition." Before 1899, founding a company in America required state legislature approval and explicit justification of a public purpose—without it, you faced criminal charges and charter revocation. Shareholder primacy only emerged after Delaware's General Corporation Law in 1899; it is recent legal doctrine, not ancient American principle.

points.h: Better governance scores consistently predict worse shareholder returns
points.body: Since 2008, data shows companies with higher governance scores underperform those with lower scores on shareholder returns. Costco rates poorly on governance; Patagonia would rank worst if rated. The shareholder primacy system defines "a company that can't be pushed around by shareholders" as bad governance—so the entire industry rewards weak leadership, weak structure, weak culture, the opposite of what most people think leadership should be.

points.h: Doing right is harder work, but ultimately the easier path
points.body: Organizations normalize saying "it's too hard to do the right thing; customers won't notice if we shortcut them," treating this as best practice. Companies rank everything by ROI, while "not harming customers" yields invisible returns against visible costs. Ries argues this systematically undervalues the most overlooked asset: trustworthiness. An organization without trust cannot endure.

points.h: Google lost one to ten trillion dollars abandoning "don't be evil"
points.body: Google invented Transformer technology, but all eight original paper authors left Google before commercialization; Ilya declined Google's $6 million annual salary to "go work with the good people." Ries argues that losing the "don't be evil" principle wasn't just moral cost—it was economic disaster. Depending on calculation method, this cost Google one to ten trillion dollars in opportunity loss.

points.h: Companies are humanity's first true AI, trained with antisocial values
points.body: Ries frames AI governance as an extension of company governance: every line of AI code originates from a company, and companies are humanity's first real artificial intelligence. We currently train them using "antisocial personality" best practices, then let these companies train AI itself. The solution isn't hoarding gold and guns for apocalypse—it's urgently changing how we govern companies to prevent technical failure.

quotes.text: Companies that have been rated to have good governance have performed worse for their shareholders than companies rated to have bad governance. Costco has terrible governance. Patagonia, if it was rated, would have the worst possible governance.
It was their very success that led to their failure. It was scale that ultimately was their undoing.
We're all one acquisition, one IPO, one board meeting away from watching something we love turn into something we hate.
They violate these, these outliers, which are multitudinous, violate practically every conventional business best practice we've been taught.
If companies cannot be instantaneously bullied to do whatever shareholders demand, that's considered bad governance. So we glorify weak leadership, weak structure, weak cultures.
This is not that kind of disaster. This is not something you prep for. This is something you have to prevent.
Corporations are the very first artificial intelligence we ever had on this planet. And we're not doing it well because we're teaching them this sociopathic set of best practices.
